198: Commerce's meaningful difference test: comparing zeroed A-T rates with non-zeroed A-A rates was a reasonable way to decide whether the A-A method could account for targeting, so the A-T method was properly used.

We agree with the CIT that Commerce's decision to compare a zeroed A-T rate with a non-zeroed A-A rate reasonably achieved the statutory goal of determining whether the A-A method could account for targeting.
199: De minimis benchmark (0.5 percent) as a basis for finding a meaningful difference between A-A and A-T rates was reasonable.
Consequently, we agree with the CIT that Commerce's de minimis benchmark was a reasonable basis for illustrating a meaningful difference between the A-A and A-T rates.
200: Application of the A-T methodology to all of Apex's sales, rather than only the sales passing the Nails test, was consistent with the statute and reasonable; the Limiting Rule did not bind Commerce in reviews.
We agree with the CIT that Commerce's application of the A-T methodology to all of Apex's sales was consistent with the statute and reasonable.
201: Use of zeroing coextensively with the A-T methodology across all of Apex's sales, rather than only targeted sales, was reasonable and adequately supported.
Commerce's use of zeroing coextensively with its use of the A-T methodology is reasonable and adequately supported.
221: AD margin calculation: on remand, Commerce properly applied the Limiting Regulation to limit average-to-transaction methodology to targeted sales, yielding a de minimis margin and 0% duty for Precision.
Mid Continent's argument that Commerce misapplied the Limiting Regulation in the agency's remand redetermination is without merit.
554: AD/CVD margin calculation: Commerce's treatment of steel retorts as factory overhead rather than direct materials in constructing normal value, upheld as supported by substantial evidence and not contrary to law.
We agree with the Trade Court that Commerce's decision was supported by substantial evidence and not otherwise contrary to law.
565: Surrogate value for the green tube factor of production: Commerce reasonably selected Indian import data under HTS 7304.59.20 as the best available information over the alternative surrogate values, rejecting claims that the value was aberrantly high.
Substantial evidence supports Commerce's selection of the surrogate value for green tube.
689: Commerce's determination to deny separate rate status and treat Dongtai Peak as part of the China-wide entity (government control presumption), resulting in the higher China-wide rate.

Here, substantial evidence supports Commerce's determination that Dongtai Peak failed to demonstrate the absence of de facto and de jure government control, as required for separate-rate status, and therefore that the company is part of the China-wide entity.
731: Commerce's use of the average-to-transaction comparison method in an administrative review after a targeted dumping finding, held a reasonable gap-filling interpretation under Chevron
Thus, contrary to JBF RAK's claims, Commerce's decision to apply its average-to-transaction comparison methodology in the context of an administrative review is reasonable.
732: Whether the statute requires Commerce to consider the reasons for a targeted pricing pattern (no intent requirement; Nails test reasonably determines a pattern)

Section 1677f-1(d)(1)(B) does not require Commerce to determine the reasons why there is a pattern of export prices for comparable merchandise that differs significantly among purchasers, regions, or time periods
923: Separate-rate calculation for non-individually investigated Chinese exporters: whether Commerce could depart from the expected method of weight-averaging zero/de minimis margins without the required findings of unrepresentativeness.

Because Commerce has not made the findings necessary to justify departing from the 'expected method' here, we vacate the judgment of the Court of International Trade, and we remand with instructions to remand to Commerce for it to reconsider its separate-rate determination.
1122: AD margin calculation: separate rate for Cherishmet and Shanxi. Commerce's carry-forward of prior-review margin rather than averaging de minimis margins of individually examined respondents was arbitrary and unsupported by substantial evidence; affirmed.
Commerce's conclusion was arbitrary and unsupported by substantial evidence. Accordingly, we affirm the CIT with respect to Cherishmet and Shanxi.
1123: AD margin calculation: separate rate for Huahui. Commerce's carry-forward of Huahui's prior-review rate ($0.44/kg) rather than averaging de minimis margins was unreasonable; reversed and remanded.

It was unreasonable under these circumstances for Commerce to reassign Huahui in the third review its rate calculated during the second review rather than take the average of the de minimis margins assigned to Jacobi and CCT.
1390: Whether Commerce's no-zeroing policy, adopted in the Final Modification, applies to the dumping margin calculation in this pending investigation. Court held the policy did not apply, so zeroing continued and duties stayed higher.
We uphold Commerce's determination, because Commerce spoke ambiguously on the timing issue in adopting its new policy and Commerce reasonably resolved the ambiguity to exclude the present matter.
1400: Duty drawback adjustment under 19 U.S.C. 1677a(c)(1)(B): Commerce's threshold test denying the adjustment where the exempted non-J55 coils could not be inputs to the subject merchandise was held a reasonable interpretation under Chevron, so the export price was not increased and the dumping margin stayed higher.
Ultimately, Commerce's interpretation was entirely reasonable and its denial of Çayirova's duty drawback adjustment was proper.
1443: Commerce's surrogate value for carbonized material (choice between Philippine HTS 4402 import data and Cocommunity coconut shell charcoal data), including the regional-data and aberrational-data critiques, upheld under substantial evidence.
Substantial evidence supports Commerce's selection of the Philippine import data to calculate the surrogate value for carbonized material.
1444: Commerce's surrogate value for truck freight (Philippine freight data over Thai freight data) upheld under substantial evidence.
Substantial evidence supported Commerce's selection of the contemporaneous, albeit less representative, Philippine freight data over the Thai freight data.
1741: Application of the recalculated PRC-wide entity rate of 82.05% to ATM in the second administrative review, affirmed on the reasoning of the companion opinion in Diamond Sawblades I.
For the reasons explained in our opinion in Diamond Sawblades I, we affirm the CIT's decision upholding Commerce's final remand redetermination applying the recalculated PRC-wide entity rate to ATM.
1847: Commerce's use of the average-to-transaction targeted dumping methodology under 19 U.S.C. § 1677f-1(d)(1)(B) to calculate the dumping margin, without considering the respondent's alternate explanation for the price pattern
We thus agree with the JBF RAK panel that Commerce's interpretation of § 1677f-1(d)(1)(B) is reasonable.
1895: AD/CVD margin calculation: corroboration requirement under 19 U.S.C. 1677e(c) held inapplicable to primary information used as adverse facts available, so Commerce need not corroborate Shinkong's margin.
Commerce properly found that § 1677e(c) unambiguously does not require the agency to corroborate information obtained during the course of the subject segment
2114: Antidumping margin methodology: Commerce's meaningful-difference test under 19 U.S.C. 1677f-1(d)(1)(B), comparing A-A without zeroing against A-T with zeroing, and its use of A-T with zeroing for Devi, were held reasonable, so higher duties were sustained.
We affirm Commerce's decision to analyze all of Devi's and Falcon's sales in conducting its meaningful difference analysis as a reasonable exercise of its delegated authority.
2115: Antidumping margin calculation for the mixed alternative methodology: Commerce's decision to zero the negative A-A margin at the aggregation step (double zeroing) for Falcon was held a reasonable methodological choice, so the higher 3.01 percent rate was sustained.
Commerce's decision to preserve the maximum amount masked dumping by zeroing the negative A-A margin was a reasonable exercise of its delegated authority, to which we defer.
2231: Commerce's recalculation of the PRC-wide entity antidumping rate (simple average of prior 164.09% rate and ATM's 0.15% margin yielding 82.12%) and whether that calculation is supported by substantial evidence and in accordance with law; NME presumption of government control applied to ATM.
Commerce's actions are supported by substantial evidence and are not contrary to law.
2913: Surrogate country selection: Commerce's exclusion of India as a surrogate country candidate under the statute and its past-practice argument, a statutory interpretation question reviewed under Chevron.
We hold that Commerce’s past practice alone of selecting India as the surrogate country does not restrain Commerce from selecting a country other than India to serve as the surrogate country.
2914: Surrogate country selection: Commerce's selection of Thailand over the Philippines as primary surrogate country for normal value, including use of the CEN financial statement, emphasis on steel inputs, and Thai HCl import data, upheld as supported by substantial evidence.
We conclude that Commerce’s selection of Thailand over the Philippines as the surrogate country is reasonable and supported by substantial evidence.
2917: Commerce's original finding that the Turkish HRS market was distorted by government involvement, which led to using world prices and a 15.58% subsidy rate; the court affirmed vacatur of that finding, so the lower 2.08% Turkish-price subsidy stands
Therefore, Commerce's original finding was not supported by substantial evidence.
3498: Weight calculation: Commerce used customer-estimated packing-slip weights rather than manufacturer-reported component weights to compute surrogate-value inputs; court held the choice unsupported by substantial evidence and reversed.
We therefore reverse the Court of International Trade's affirmance of that choice and direct Commerce to use the manufacturer-reported weights in its calculation.
3499: Korean subsidies: Commerce's presumption-based rejection of CS Wind's Korean purchase prices in favor of Indian surrogate values for flanges, welding wire and wire flux; court held substantial evidence supported it and affirmed.
We conclude that substantial evidence supports Commerce's conclusion that CS Wind did not make its case.
3595: Surrogate value selection for steel billets (simple average of carbon and alloy steel surrogate values) used in calculating Chengde's dumping margin
We agree with the Trade Court and the Appellees that substantial evidence supports Commerce's decision to use an average surrogate value of carbon steel and alloy steel.
3596: Denial of byproduct (steel scrap) offset in the dumping margin calculation for failure to document scrap produced
We agree with the Trade Court and the Appellees that Commerce did not err in declining to allow any scrap offset in this case.
3597: Valuation of international ocean freight as a nonmarket economy input using a surrogate value rather than the market economy carrier price
We agree with the Trade Court and the Appellees that Commerce properly calculated Chengde's ocean freight expenses using a surrogate value.
3895: Subsidy calculation: whether Commerce's broad preferentiality-based position (nondiscriminatory, consistently set rate suffices for adequate remuneration) is a lawful reading of the less-than-adequate-remuneration standard; court rejected it, which favors higher duties.
That position is beyond any reasonable interpretation of the statute, or of its implementing regulation.
3896: Subsidy calculation: court upheld Commerce's finding that KEPCO's electricity pricing met adequate remuneration based on cost recovery, so no countervailable subsidy from electricity sales; favors lower duties.
We have been shown no reversible error in Commerce's decision to rely on that combination of facts as sufficient to meet the adequate remuneration standard.
3916: Commerce's methodology under 19 U.S.C. § 1677b(a)(6)(C)(iii) and 19 C.F.R. § 351.410(e): denial of a home market commission offset where no commissions were incurred in the home market or outside the U.S. on U.S. sales, and commissions were incurred inside the U.S. on CEP sales; the court held this reasonable, leaving the higher margin in place.
Like the Court of International Trade, we conclude that Commerce’s approach represents a reasonable construction of 19 U.S.C. § 1677b(a)(6)(C)(iii).
4390: CVD benefit-conferred methodology: Commerce's reliance on a preferential-rate standard to find no benefit from electricity provided for less than adequate remuneration was contrary to law; vacated and remanded.

Consistent with our holding in Nucor, we hold that Commerce's reliance on a preferential-rate standard is inconsistent with the Trade statute, in particular with the less-than-adequate-remuneration requirement, and is therefore contrary to law.
4392: CVD subsidy calculation: Commerce failed to investigate and consider KPX's role and generation costs in the adequate-remuneration (cost recovery) analysis; final determination unsupported by substantial evidence and contrary to law; vacated and remanded.
Commerce's failure to treat KPX as an authority—or, at a minimum, investigate whether it is an authority—constitutes error as a matter of law.
4416: Surrogate value for Trina's nitrogen input based on Thai GTA import data; Commerce did not adequately justify use of the aberrational data, so the CIT judgment sustaining it is vacated and remanded (favors lower duties for Trina).
We agree with Trina that Commerce has not provided a persuasive reason for using the Thai GTA data in light of unrebutted evidence of its unreliability.
4417: Use of zero-quantity import records in calculating average unit values; the court did not reach whether the practice was correct and affirmed because Trina showed no harm.
We affirm the CIT's decision to sustain Commerce's use of zero-quantity data because Trina has failed to demonstrate that the alleged error, if there was an error, was harmful.
4418: Selection of Thai HTS subheadings 3920.62 and 3920.10 to value Yingli's and Trina's backsheets rather than SolarWorld's proposed subheading 3920.99; court found Commerce's choice supported by substantial evidence.
Commerce's reasonable choice of the more specific HTS categories is supported by substantial evidence.
4419: Use of Thai GTA data to value Yingli's tempered glass input, affected by aberrational Hong Kong imports; court affirmed the CIT's remand requiring Commerce to further explain or reconsider.
We affirm the CIT's remand to Commerce to further explain or reconsider its decision to use the Thai GTA data to value Yingli's tempered glass input.
4558: Commerce's selection of the South African Oceana Report, rather than Thai financial statements, to calculate surrogate financial ratios for the dumping margin calculation; upheld as supported by substantial evidence and in accordance with law, so margins stayed higher.
Substantial evidence supports Commerce's determination that the Oceana Report is the best available information on the record to value the surrogate financial ratios.
4945: AD/CVD margin calculation: Commerce's reliance on Dillinger's books and records, which valued non-prime plate at likely selling price, in allocating costs under 19 U.S.C. 1677b(f). Court held Commerce erred and remanded for actual cost calculation.
Because Dillinger's books and records were based on "likely selling price" rather than cost of production, id., Commerce erred in relying on them.
4946: AD/CVD margin calculation: Commerce's use of the average-to-transaction method based on its Cohen's d and ratio test showing a pattern of prices differing significantly among purchasers, regions or periods. Court upheld the pattern determination as a reasonable interpretation.
We find that Commerce's interpretation of pattern was reasonable.
4948: AD/CVD margin calculation: Commerce's determination that Dillinger's factory and service center sales were a single level of trade, so no level-of-trade adjustment to normal value was warranted. Court affirmed.
We see no error in Commerce's refusal to consider these processing activities to be selling functions.
5117: Constructed value methodology: Commerce's rejection of the preferred profit/SG&A method as lacking viable home-market sales, and the 'available' determination under 19 U.S.C. 1677b(e)(2).
we affirm the Trade Court with respect to OF's challenge to Commerce's rejection of the method set forth in 19 U.S.C. § 1677b(e)(2)(A).
5119: Selection of Hitech (Thai screw producer) as the surrogate source of profit data over LSI and Omani companies, apart from the subsidies issue.
we conclude that Commerce's application of the statute was reasonable on the record here.
5120: Commerce's refusal to consider whether subsidies to Hitech distorted its profits when borrowing Hitech's profit data for constructed value.
On this issue, we agree with OF; Commerce's explanation is wanting.
5121: Refusal to calculate a profit cap under 19 U.S.C. 1677b(e)(2)(B)(iii) because no suitable home-market data or facts available existed.
We therefore affirm the Trade Court's rejection of OF's challenge on the profit-cap determination.
5301: Commerce's collapsing of Prosperity, Yieh and Synn into a single entity under 19 C.F.R. 351.401(f) held contrary to law and unsupported by substantial evidence because Commerce failed to consider the totality of circumstances across all entity pairs; vacated.

We conclude that Commerce acted contrary to law when it collapsed Prosperity, Yieh, and Synn without considering the § 351.401(f) factors as between the relationships of Prosperity and Yieh or between Prosperity and Yieh/Synn.
5335: AD margin calculation: Commerce's treatment of X. Campestris as an asset rather than a direct material input and selection of surrogate financial statements (Thai Ajinomoto vs. Thai Fermentation) for surrogate financial ratios; court affirmed treatment as asset (higher-duty outcome for CP Kelco rejected) and reinstated Thai Ajinomoto statements.

We affirm the Trade Court's decision to uphold Commerce's treatment of X. Campestris as an asset. We reverse its decision regarding Commerce's use of the Thai Fermentation financial statements to calculate surrogate financial ratios and reinstate Commerce's determination to use the Ajinomoto (Thailand) Co., Ltd. (Thai Ajinomoto) financial statements.
5623: Whether the CVD rate applicable to Capella's pre-Timken-notice entries is the 374.15% rate from Commerce's final determination or the lower 7.37% rate from the MacLean-Fogg litigation; court held Commerce's final determination rate governs under 19 U.S.C. 1516a(c)(1) and Chevron deference to 19 C.F.R. 351.212(c).
we conclude that Capella's pre-Timken notice entries not enjoined by court order under § 1516a(c)(2) may properly be "liquidated as entered" in accordance with the Secretary's final determination.
5662: Commerce's methodology for valuing the fish oil by-product offset in the constructed normal value (rejecting Indonesian HTS data and using constructed value from Vinh Hoan's own factors of production); upheld as supported by substantial evidence and not contrary to law.
Because we find Commerce's methodology was supported by substantial evidence and neither arbitrary or capricious or contrary to the law, the decision of the CIT is AFFIRMED
6299: AD margin calculation: Commerce's selection of a surrogate value for Yingli's aluminum frames (Thai HTS Heading 7604 import data) was supported by substantial evidence, leaving the margin lower.
Substantial evidence supports Commerce's finding that import data under Thai HTS Heading 7604 constitutes the best available information from which to value Yingli's aluminum frames.
6300: AD margin calculation: Commerce's selection of the world market price for polysilicon as the surrogate value for semi-finished ingots and blocks was supported by substantial evidence, leaving the margin lower.
We conclude that substantial evidence supports Commerce's finding that the world market price was the best available information on the record.
6379: Affiliation determination under 19 U.S.C. §1677(33) for toll manufacturers used in constructed value; Commerce's finding of non-affiliation (ability to control) sustained against Mid Continent's challenge.
We therefore affirm Commerce's determination that PT and the toll manufacturers at issue in the appeal are not affiliated.
6380: Zeroing of negative-margin sales in the A-to-A group at the aggregation stage; PT's statutory challenge rejected and Commerce's zeroing upheld.
We therefore reject the only challenge PT makes to Commerce's use of zeroing in the identified part of its calculation.
6381: Use of a Cohen's d coefficient of 0.8 as a rigid threshold for significant price differences in the differential pricing analysis; PT's flexibility challenge rejected.
We agree with the Trade Court that this rationale adequately supports Commerce's exercise of the wide discretion left to it under 19 U.S.C. § 1677f1(d)(1)(B).
7000: AD margin calculation: whether Commerce properly declined to offset Trina's export price by the countervailed Ex-Im Bank Buyer's Credit subsidy (export price offset under 19 U.S.C. 1677a(c)(1)(C)); held Commerce's refusal contrary to law, so the offset applies, lowering the margin.
Commerce's decision to not offset Trina's export price, based on its reliance on AFA to countervail the Ex-Im Bank Buyer's Credit Program, is contrary to law.
7001: AD/CVD margin methodology: surrogate value selection for Trina's module glass (Thai HTS 7007.19.90000 tempered glass) supported by substantial evidence and best available information, sustaining the valuation.
Accordingly, substantial evidence supports Commerce's decision to value Trina's module glass using Thai imports of tempered glass classified under HTS Subheading 7007.19.90000.
7010: Surrogate financial ratios: Commerce's selection of Bhushan's financial statements as surrogate financial ratios for SeAH's normal value was supported by substantial evidence and in accordance with law.
Substantial evidence supports Commerce's determination that Bhushan's financial statements are the best available information on the record to calculate SeAH's surrogate financial ratios.
7011: Inland insurance surrogate value: Commerce's inclusion of a separate surrogate value for domestic inland insurance was supported by substantial evidence and in accordance with law.
Accordingly, Commerce's inclusion of a separate surrogate value for inland insurance is supported by substantial evidence and otherwise in accordance with law.
7012: By-weight allocation methodology for brokerage and handling (B&H) surrogate costs was unsupported by substantial evidence as applied, so the margin calculation was remanded.
We agree with SeAH that Commerce's by-weight allocation methodology for B&H costs is, as applied here, unsupported by substantial evidence.
7344: Commerce's selection of HTS Heading 7604 as the surrogate value for the aluminum frame factor inputs in the antidumping margin calculation, affirmed as supported by substantial evidence.
We affirm the CIT's decision that 'Commerce's use of subheading 7604.29.65, HTS, to value respondents' aluminum frames is supported by substantial evidence.'
7345: Commerce's practice of offsetting the antidumping cash deposit rate by the countervailing duty rate for export subsidies, which lowers the AD rate, held a reasonable implementation of the statute under Chevron.
We have considered the concerns raised by SolarWorld, and conclude that Commerce's practice with respect to offset of cash deposit rates reasonably implements the statute.
7991: AD margin calculation methodology: Commerce properly rejected Pioneer's non-CONNUM-specific FOP data under the Tariff Act and Hynix, so the methodology stood and the higher duty margin resulted.
On this record, we agree with, and therefore affirm, the Court of International Trade's determination that Commerce's conclusion was based on substantial evidence.
7997: Particular market situation finding under 19 U.S.C. 1677b(e) for constructed value: Commerce's finding was unsupported by substantial evidence, so Commerce's constructed-value cost adjustment is not sustained and the lower-duty outcome stands.
We affirm the Court of International Trade's conclusions in NEXTEEL II that three of the circumstances Commerce cited do not support a finding of a particular market situation on the existing record.
7999: Differential pricing analysis (Cohen's d, average-to-transaction comparison) used to calculate dumping margins: upheld by CIT, vacated and remanded in view of Stupp.

We vacate the Court of International Trade's decision upholding Commerce's differential pricing analysis for the reasons stated in our recent decision in Stupp, 5 F.4th 1341, and remand for proceedings consistent with that decision.
8000: Freight revenue cap in export price adjustment under 19 U.S.C. 1677a(c)(2)(A): Commerce's methodology capping freight revenue at freight expense was held reasonable.
Commerce's freight revenue cap methodology is reasonable. We thus affirm the Court of International Trade's decision upholding Commerce's methodology.
8001: Profit cap for constructed value under 19 U.S.C. 1677b(e)(2)(B)(iii): Commerce's use of SeAH's own Canadian sales as facts available for the profit cap was held lawful.
We thus affirm the holding of the Court of International Trade that Commerce's application of the profit cap is lawful.
8478: Commerce's selection of Malaysia as the primary surrogate country for valuing factors of production in the AR11 antidumping review, upheld as supported by substantial evidence.
Commerce's selection of Malaysia as the primary surrogate country is supported by substantial evidence and not otherwise contrary to law.
8480: Commerce's valuation of coal tar pitch using Malaysian import statistics under HS 2708.10 rather than Russian HS 2706.00 data, upheld.
Collectively, this is substantial evidence for Commerce's conclusion.
8482: Commerce's valuation of bituminous coal with a known calorific value using Malaysian HS 2701.19 import data, upheld.
Thus, we agree with the CIT that Commerce's decision to use Malaysian import statistics for bituminous coal having a known calorific value is supported by substantial evidence.
8483: Commerce's valuation of bituminous coal with an unknown calorific value using Romanian HS 2701.12 import data, upheld.
Accordingly, we agree with the CIT that Commerce's decision to value bituminous coal with an unknown calorific value under Romanian HS 2701.12 is supported by substantial evidence.
8586: Antidumping margin methodology: application of the China-wide 114.90% rate to the importer Prime Time as Ningbo Homey's corresponding importer, supported by substantial evidence; the court found Commerce's failure to consider the importer's cooperation harmless error.
Under the framework of the presumption and requirement to rebut government control, the China-wide rate of 114.90% would nonetheless be applied to Prime Time’s entries.
8670: AD margin calculation: whether Commerce properly limited the post-sale price adjustment to the one-third initial allocation rather than Borusan's final allocated penalty share, so the margin stays at 5.11 percent.

We hold that Commerce's original Final Determination that Borusan was entitled to a post-sale price adjustment based on the one-third initial allocation agreed to by the JVA members because the one-third allocation was known and established at the time of sale is supported by substantial evidence and in accordance with the law.
8729: Regional specificity of the Chinese electricity subsidy under 19 U.S.C. 1677(5A)(D)(iv) held supported by substantial evidence, so the subsidy is countervailable.

We agree with the CIT that, where documents support the inference that the central government of China was involved in provincial electricity pricing that results in regional price variability, substantial evidence supports Commerce's finding that there is a countervailable regionally specific subsidy.
8730: Benchmark used in the subsidy rate calculation (highest provincial electricity rate as unsubsidized benchmark) held reasonable.
In the absence of that information, it was reasonable for Commerce to infer that the highest rate in each category was unsubsidized.
9013: Denial of separate antidumping rate to Qixin in administrative review, leaving Qixin at the PRC-wide (higher) rate for the 2014-2015 review period.
Qixin simply failed to resolve an ambiguity necessary for it to secure relief.
9100: Commerce's export price calculation: subtracting RIN value as a price adjustment under 19 C.F.R. 351.401(c) and 351.102(b)(38); court held regulation unambiguously permits the subtraction.
We agree with Commerce that 19 C.F.R. §§ 351.401(c) and 351.102(b)(38) allow it to subtract the value of RINs from export price as a "price adjustment."
9101: Substantial evidence supporting the value Commerce used for RINs (separated RINs spot price as proxy for attached RINs).
This statement, which LDC does not acknowledge in its briefing, provides substantial evidence to support Commerce's use of the separated RINs price.
9102: Constructed normal value: particular market situation adjustment under 19 U.S.C. 1677b(e) using international soybean prices; court held no double remedy and affirmed Commerce's finding of no pass-through of the soybean subsidy.
We affirm Commerce's finding that there is no risk of double counting in this case.
9164: Whether Commerce properly treated the Proclamation 9705 Section 232 duty as a 'United States import duty' to be subtracted from U.S. price in calculating the dumping margin (AD margin methodology).
Because Commerce correctly determined that the particular § 232 duty imposed by Proclamation 9705 is a "United States import dut[y]" under 19 U.S.C. § 1677a(c)(2)(A), we affirm.
9278: Reasonableness of the ratio test and its 33% and 66% cutoffs used to choose the average-to-transaction method in the dumping margin calculation
we hold that Commerce's ratio test reasonably implements the statutory requirement that Commerce determine whether there is a pattern of export prices differing significantly
9279: Reasonableness of Commerce's meaningful difference test used to confirm use of the alternative comparison method
Accordingly, we affirm Commerce's use of the meaningful difference test.
9418: CVD benefit determination: whether KEPCO's provision of electricity to Korean steel producers was for less than adequate remuneration under the post-URAA prevailing-market standard, so that no countervailing duty applied. The court sustained Commerce's remand determination of no benefit.
Because we agree with the trial court that the agency's remand determination complies with our decision in POSCO, we affirm.
9423: Commerce's inclusion of 20 disputed subsidy programs in calculating Uttam Galva's countervailable subsidy rate, based on its affiliation with LSIL.
We therefore conclude that Commerce's inclusion of the 20 disputed programs is supported by substantial evidence.
9602: Commerce's determination that Zhejiang failed to rebut the presumption of de facto government control and was denied a separate antidumping rate, leaving the country-wide rate in place (closest fit: dumping margin methodology).

Commerce's determination that Zhejiang was not entitled to a separate rate was reasonable and supported by substantial evidence because a labor union is the majority shareholder with significant rights over Zhejiang and has overlapping membership with the employee stock-ownership committee.
9901: Commerce's methodology for the duty drawback adjustment to export price: whether Commerce could allocate the drawback between U.S. exports and home-market sales. The court held the statute requires the full drawback to increase export price, so Commerce's allocation was unlawful.
There is no basis for doing so.
10006: Commerce's dumping-margin methodology: under 19 U.S.C. 1677(c)(2) Commerce erred by determining the all-others rate from a single mandatory respondent, and the resulting rate applied to other separate-rate respondents was therefore unsupported by substantial evidence. Judgment vacated and remanded.
We conclude that Commerce erred in restricting its examination to only one exporter/producer.
10398: Reasonableness of Commerce's 41.025% separate antidumping margin in light of historical dumping rates; court held the rate supported by substantial evidence and upheld it.
we conclude that Commerce's calculation of the 41.025% rate was supported by substantial evidence.
10523: Interpretation of 'substantially dependent' under 19 U.S.C. § 1677-2 as the basis for attributing Spanish olive subsidies to processed table olives; court holds the statute does not require at least 50 percent and affirms Commerce's flexible holistic standard.
Because Commerce's findings satisfy the statutory requirements of section 1677–2 and are supported by substantial evidence, we sustain the Trade Court's decision.
10524: Commerce's subsidy-attribution calculation yielding 55.28 percent dependence; court finds arithmetic errors in treatment of cacereña and other dual-use varietals but holds them nonprejudicial and no remand required, so the higher duty stands.
Although Commerce erred in its treatment of cacereña and “other” dual-use varietal olives, the error did not have a significant effect on the percentage calculation.
10575: AD/CVD margin calculation: Commerce's use of simple averaging for the pooled standard deviation (denominator) in the Cohen's d test used for the differential pricing and average-to-transaction analysis was not adequately justified; the court vacated the Trade Court's sustaining decision and remanded.
We hold that Commerce has not adequately justified its adoption of simple averaging for the Cohen's d denominator.
10734: Whether Commerce could make a particular market situation (PMS) adjustment to the cost of production when calculating antidumping margins; the court held it could not, so margins were calculated without the adjustment.
Hyundai Steel is indistinguishable from this case and is controlling.
10919: Whether Commerce may adjust respondents' costs of production for a particular market situation (PMS) in the sales-below-cost test; held not authorized under the 2015 TPEA amendments (Chevron step one), so the dumping margin calculation stands.
we disagree with Commerce's interpretation of the statute, and for the reasons set forth below, we hold that Commerce's interpretation fails at Chevron step one.
10965: Commerce's assignment of the 105.31% PRC-wide entity rate to Double Coin, calculated by averaging the carried-forward AFA-based rate with Double Coin's 0.14% rate; court held the rate lawful, reversing the Trade Court's bar on applying it.
we conclude that Commerce was within the law in assigning the 105.31% PRC-wide entity rate to Double Coin.
11318: Commerce's use of the expected method (weight-averaging AFA rates) to calculate the all-others AD rate for non-selected respondents, with no affirmative Commerce burden to show reasonableness; 78.17% all-others rate sustained

Commerce's decision to apply the expected method, resulting in a 78.17% all-others rate, to the non-selected respondents was therefore supported by substantial evidence and in accordance with the law.
11320: Denial of an individual (voluntary respondent) rate to Liang Chyuan, which it could not obtain because its willingness letter came too late under 19 U.S.C. 1677m(a)
Commerce's decision to not grant Liang Chyuan an individual rate was therefore in accordance with the law.
11402: AD margin calculation methodology: substantial evidence supports Commerce's use of the intermediate input methodology to measure Chengen's factors of production, yielding a 183.36% margin; Trade Court's contrary determination was reversed.
Substantial evidence supports Commerce's finding that the same is true here for Chengen's use of poplar logs.
11453: Whether Commerce lawfully assigned the NME-wide (PRC-wide) antidumping rate of 25.62% to Jilin, a cooperative respondent that failed to rebut the NME presumption of government control, and whether that NME policy required notice-and-comment rulemaking.
Accordingly, CMA and the long line of cases CMA relied on are binding precedent that Jilin may not avoid unless or until the court sits en banc.
11638: AD/CVD margin and rate methodology: Commerce's use of a rebuttable presumption of government control and treatment of the de facto control factors for separate-rate eligibility, upheld under Pirelli Tyre.
This contention cannot prevail in light of our decision in Pirelli Tyre, issued after the briefing in the matters before us here was complete.
11832: Cost smoothing (weight-averaging) of Marmen's steel plate costs under the cost-of-production rules; Commerce's methodology was upheld as consistent with its practice and supported by substantial evidence.
Commerce did not act arbitrarily or inconsistently with its standard practice.
11833: Rejection of Marmen's USD-to-CAD exchange-rate cost-reconciliation correction in the margin calculation; the court held the rejection was not supported by substantial evidence.
Thus, we conclude that Commerce's determination that the exchange rate would double count records or is unreliable is not supported by substantial evidence.
11834: Use of the average-to-transaction margin methodology based on Cohen's d test; the court held reliance on Cohen's d for non-normal, unequal-variance data was unreasonable and vacated the resulting margin.
We therefore vacate Commerce's calculated dumping margin based on the unreasonable use of Cohen's d test to justify the A-to-T methodology.
12144: Model-match methodology for protein content: Commerce's failure to account for FDA rounding rules and different nitrogen-to-protein conversion factors in CONNUM coding violated the identical-physical-characteristics requirement of 19 U.S.C. 1677(16)(A); vacated and remanded.

For the reasons stated above, we conclude that Commerce's determinations regarding rounding and nitrogen conversion factors are not supported by substantial evidence. Therefore, we vacate the Trade Court's judgment in these respects and remand for further proceedings consistent with this opinion.
12145: Whether the Market Report and Bologna Grain Exchange 13.5 percent breakpoint constituted a compelling reason to change the 12.5 percent standard/premium protein breakpoint; Commerce's refusal to change it was sustained.
Because a reasonable mind could conclude that La Molisana failed to present compelling evidence of a change in the protein breakpoint, we affirm the judgment of the Trade Court on this issue.
12194: De facto specificity: Commerce had reasonable flexibility to choose the comparator group in the predominant user analysis under 19 U.S.C. 1677(5A)(D)(iii)(II), and its predominant usage finding was reasonable, so the subsidy was specific.
we hold that under 19 U.S.C. § 1677(5A)(D)(iii)(II), Commerce has reasonable flexibility in assessing predominant usage.
12195: LTAR benchmark: Commerce properly used Mosaic's IEA data as a tier three benchmark, considered government-created market distortion, and was not required by 19 U.S.C. 1677(5)(E)(iv) to adjust the data for natural gas abundance.
we determine that Commerce’s LTAR determination is in accordance with the tier three framework at 19 C.F.R. § 351.511(a)(2)(iii) and with 19 U.S.C. § 1677(5)(E)(iv).
12278: Whether Commerce properly determined that the exporter did not reimburse the affiliated importer for antidumping duties, which affects the export price/constructed export price calculation and dumping margin; court held the determination was supported by substantial evidence and in accordance with law, and that Commerce did not depart from established practice in failing to apply the reimbursement regulation.
we hold that the agency's determination was supported by substantial evidence and was otherwise in accordance with law.
12303: Whether Commerce properly attributed a non-party input producer's land-lease subsidy to Gujarat under the cross-ownership regulation, 19 C.F.R. § 351.525(b)(6)(iv), which the court held inapplicable, so the 26.50% CVD rate could not stand.
we agree that 19 C.F.R. § 351.525(b)(6)(iv) was inapplicable under the circumstances in this case and therefore affirm.
12395: Surrogate country selection and surrogate financial ratios (Malaysia as primary surrogate; Century and Bravo Green financial statements), AR13 dumping margin methodology
Under this standard, based upon the evidence it had before it, we see no error in Commerce's selection of the financial statements of Century and Bravo Green over those of Romcarbon and JSC Sorbent.
12396: Surrogate value of coal-based carbonized material using coconut shell charcoal HTS 4402.90.1000 data (non-contemporaneous, adjusted twelfth-review data)
We agree with the Trade Court's rejection of Carbon Activated's argument on this point.
12397: Surrogate value of coal tar using Malaysian HTS 2706.00 import data
Again, we see no error in this ruling.
12398: Surrogate value of hydrochloric acid using Malaysian HTS 2806.10 basket data rather than Brazilian aqueous subheading data
We see no reason to disturb that finding and thus see no merit in Carbon Activated's arguments that Commerce should have used a more specific subheading or more specific data.
12399: Surrogate value of steam using Malaysian liquified natural gas HTS 2711.11 import data
Carbon Activated has failed to demonstrate any error in the Trade Court's reasoning on this point.
12400: Surrogate value of ocean freight using Maersk tariff data rather than Descartes data
None of them has convinced us that the Trade Court erred in concluding that Commerce's decision with respect to freight charges was supported by substantial evidence and was free of legal error.
12839: AD/CVD margin calculation: Commerce's choice to calculate normal value using Habaş's lira-denominated home-market sales, rather than dollar prices, and the resulting 24.32 percent dumping margin, upheld as lawful and supported by substantial evidence.
We hold that Commerce's reliance on Habaş's lira-denominated sales to calculate normal value comports with Commerce's statutory obligations.
12853: Countervailable benefit from the first three equity infusions: whether Commerce's finding of benefit (government domination, insignificant private investor participation, unequityworthiness) was supported by substantial evidence
We therefore conclude that Commerce’s finding of countervailable benefit associated with the first three equity infusions is supported by substantial evidence.
12854: Pass-through of the non-recurring subsidy benefit to KG Consortium after acquisition: whether the baseline presumption of pass-through and the rebuttal of arm's length fair-market-value sale were supported by substantial evidence
we cannot say that Commerce’s determination of pass-through based on the established presumption was error.
13281: AD/CVD margin calculation: Commerce's assignment of the country-wide NME antidumping rate (52.79%) to Jin Tiong for failing to file a timely separate rate application, and its withdrawal of the questionnaire and rejection of the unsolicited Section A response, were reasonable and supported by substantial evidence.
Because Jin Tiong failed to file an SRA, Commerce was within its discretion to determine Jin Tiong failed to rebut the presumption of government control.
13763: AD margin calculation: Commerce's use of Cohen's d test within its differential pricing analysis to select the comparison methodology (A-to-A, A-to-T or hybrid) for SeAH's dumping margin was unreasonable.
Accordingly, we hold that it was unreasonable for Commerce to use Cohen's d as part of its differential pricing analysis in this case.
13786: AD margin calculation: Commerce's selection of Sundram's financial statement as the surrogate profit source over Al Jazeera's, and the harmlessness of any failure to address Sundram's subsidy, sustaining the 4.22% dumping margin.

Because Sundram's financial statements were "the only contemporaneous [financial statements] on the record reflecting production, sale, and profit from the sale of comparable merchandise," J.A. 34, and "data reflecting the production and profit from sale of comparable merchandise are always preferable to a profit experience wholly dissimilar to the mandatory respondent," J.A. 39, Commerce's reliance on Sundram rather than Al Jazeera was reasonable.
13787: AD margin calculation: Commerce's refusal to rely on the partially translated LSI financial statement or to reopen the record to admit a fully translated LSI statement, as a discretionary record matter in the surrogate-value analysis.
Whether to accept the partial translation or reopen the record are within Commerce's discretion, which it did not abuse here.
13923: Commerce's adjustment of DKSC's reported steel plate input costs by weight-averaging under 19 U.S.C. 1677b(f)(1)(A), which increased the constructed cost and thus the dumping margin; upheld as supported by substantial evidence.
We thus affirm the CIT's decision upholding Commerce's input cost adjustment.
13924: Commerce's choice of SSHC's consolidated 2018 financial statement as surrogate data for constructed value profit and selling expenses under 19 U.S.C. 1677b(e)(2)(B)(iii); upheld as supported by substantial evidence.

We find that Commerce's decision to calculate constructed value profit and selling expenses using the consolidated 2018 financial statement of SSHC, rather than the standalone financial data of SeAH Steel Corporation, was supported by substantial evidence.
14046: Commerce's determination that Double Coin failed to show absence of de facto government control, so it was assigned the PRC-wide entity rate (higher duties) under the separate-rate presumption; substantial-evidence challenge rejected.
We reject that challenge on its merits and therefore need not address the government's argument that appellants' substantial-evidence challenge is foreclosed by our 2021 decision.
14144: Commerce's use of the expected method to calculate the 35.30% all-others dumping rate for non-individually examined producers Hor Liang and Romp, held supported by substantial evidence.
Commerce's use of the expected method to calculate the 35.30% all-others rate is supported by substantial evidence.
14268: Commerce's use of likely selling price as facts otherwise available in place of actual cost of production for non-prime plate (cost of production methodology). Court held this unreasonable and vacated.
it is not reasonable for Commerce to rely on likely selling price as facts otherwise available for cost of production.
14533: CVD subsidy calculation: Commerce excluded Marmen's auditor's exchange-rate adjustment from the sales denominator as unverified and unreliable, and the court affirmed.
we agree with the Court of International Trade that Commerce's exclusion of Marmen's requested auditor adjustment was supported by substantial evidence and in accordance with law.
14534: CVD countervailable subsidy finding: Commerce found the additional Class 1 depreciation allowance a financial contribution conferring a benefit.
The additional 6% allowance claimed and received by Marmen thus represents revenue that the Canadian governments could have collected but forewent, which constitutes a "financial contribution."
14535: CVD benefit calculation for the GASPÉTC tax credit: Commerce did not offset the benefit by taxes paid on the prior year's credit.

we agree with the Court of International Trade that Commerce acted in accordance with law when it excluded taxes incurred from the previous year's credit in computing the benefit Marmen received under the GASPÉTC program.
14536: CVD specificity: Commerce found the on-the-job training tax credit de facto specific based on the limited-in-number factor and its corporate-filer comparator.

we agree with the Court of International Trade that Commerce's de facto specificity determination of the on-the-job training credit is supported by substantial evidence and is otherwise in accordance with law.
14581: AD margin calculation methodology: factors-of-production surrogate valuation under NME methodology; Commerce's reliance on activation process evidence upheld, leaving higher duty rate in place

Because the physical properties of activated carbon depend not only on the input materials used, but also on the activation process, Commerce reasonably relied on the activation process for steam-activated carbon in making its surrogate value selection
14698: Surrogate value selection for backsheet and EVA inputs: Commerce's choice of Malaysian HTS 'sheet' categories over 'film' categories was supported by substantial evidence and not contrary to law, so the Trade Court's sustaining of that choice was affirmed.
Commerce's choices of the HTS categories applicable to "sheet" for Risen's backsheet and EVA inputs were supported by substantial evidence and not otherwise contrary to law.
14699: Surrogate financial ratio (overhead) calculation: Commerce's allocation of unidentified Hanwha costs to overhead was not supported by substantial evidence, so the Trade Court's judgment was vacated and remanded, favoring Risen's position that the costs belonged in materials, labor and energy.

On the present record, Commerce's allocation of the remaining 257,063 ringgits in unidentified costs to overhead appears to be based on nothing more than guesswork or speculation, not substantial evidence.
14753: Cross-attribution of countervailable subsidies to Kaptan under the primarily dedicated test; Commerce found Nur's unprocessed steel scrap was a common input and not a mere link in the production chain, and the court affirmed.
14754: Weight Commerce gave to Nur's shipbuilding business activity in the primarily dedicated analysis; the court held Commerce could consider it and found no error, affirming lower duties.
We reject RTAC's contention that the weight Commerce afforded to Nur's status as a shipbuilder was inconsistent with the regulation and Preamble.
15004: Date of sale methodology under 19 C.F.R. § 351.401(i): whether Commerce's invoice-date starting point exceeds its authority under the Tariff Act (Loper Bright challenge), which the court rejected.
Kaptan has not shown any error by the Trade Court in relation to Loper Bright.
15005: Substantial evidence challenge to Commerce's use of Kaptan's invoice date rather than the contract date as the date of sale in calculating the dumping margin (25.86% rate).
Like the Trade Court, we conclude that substantial evidence supports Commerce’s decision to use the invoice date.
15049: AD/CVD margin calculation: whether Commerce's separate-rate (de facto control) analysis and the rebuttable presumption of government control were lawful and supported by substantial evidence, resulting in the PRC-wide rate
